articles.title: The Best Family Christmas Pajama Brands: Top Picks for Prints, Fabric and Comfort
articles.content:
Our top pick: Deer Deer Pajamas
When it comes to the best family Christmas pajamas, Hanna Andersson is a tried-and-true favorite. This year, they have over 60 holiday prints to choose from, including beloved characters like Bluey and the Grinch, as well as classic plaids and stripes. Pajama sets are made of 100% cotton and are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified, meaning they’re free from harmful substances and, best of all, not made of plastic.
They are available in baby, kids’, women’s, men’s, adult unisex and pet sizes. And while they do come in sets, they’re designed to be mixed and matched. In other words, you can rock a matching set or create a holiday look that’s all your own.
Deputy editor Katie Bandurski and her family have spent the last four Christmases cozying up in Hanna Andersson’s flannel Deer Deer pajamas, and she is happy to say that they’ve held up year after year. “For my family, it’s all about feeling together and united during the holiday season. We traditionally open presents on Christmas Eve, and it’s so nice to come home, change out of church clothes and relax in something cozy while we watch It’s a Wonderful Life,” she explains in her Hanna Andersson review. “This has been our tradition for many years, and the matching PJs add a little extra flair. My sister lives out of state, so the holidays are one of our best chances to all be together.”
Before you buy, click the “sizing help” link and carefully review the measurements, as these pajamas tend to run large. “Generally, I’d say they run a bit big, which is great for that super cozy fit. After all, there’s nothing worse than tight pajamas,” Katie says. If you order the wrong size, the brand does not offer exchanges and charges a $7.50 fee for each return shipment.
Our top pick: Nostalgic Christmas Organic Cotton Pajama Set
Trying to avoid plastics and other harmful chemicals? We don’t blame you. Burt’s Bees offers a beautiful line of high-quality pajamas made from 100% organic cotton. These jammies are soft, breathable and gentle on sensitive skin, making them an excellent choice for little ones. They come in a wide selection of hand-painted, watercolor prints that will look beautiful in family photos. We especially love this Nostalgic Christmas print.
Shopping editor Mary Henn and her family wore Burt’s Bees Christmas pajamas last year, and she was impressed by the comfort and quality. “I’m a big fan of the Burt’s Bees family pajamas,” she says. “They offer a wide range of sizes and prints, from newborn onesies to dog bandanas, so every family member is included. Unlike typical button-up sets, these pajamas consist of long-sleeve shirts and pajama pants. But they’re incredibly durable and withstand multiple washes without losing their quality.”
We also appreciate the fact that these pajamas are relatively budget-friendly. Prices range from $19 for infant and toddler sizes to $50 for adult pajamas. Burt’s Bees also runs frequent sales. The only thing to keep in mind is that you have 30 days to return an item if it doesn’t live up to your expectations. However, we’re confident that you’ll love these pajamas as much as we do.
Our top pick: Let Us Adore Him Bamboo Pajama Set
Christmas truly is the most wonderful time of year. Of course, the carols, cookies, decorations and family traditions all help the season feel magical. But if your family is also intentional about remembering the real reason for the season, Holy Pals pajamas are for you. I came across these pajamas on my Instagram feed and fell in love with the message and the prints.
In addition to eight faith-inspired designs, each pajama set has a small scripture tag on the sleeve. This tag references the Bible story recounting Jesus’ birth and serves as a reminder of why we celebrate Christmas.
I ordered the brand’s Let Us Adore Him bamboo pajama set, which features a nativity-inspired design and trendy bows, and it’s just as pretty in person as it is online. Better still, they fit perfectly, are super soft, and the quality is on par with my Cozy Earth pajamas. And since clothing tags tend to bother two of my children, I appreciate the fact that Holy Pals PJs are tagless.
Our top pick: Santa Letter Cotton And Dream Fleece Henley Pajamas
As a mom of four, believe me when I say that buying multiple sets of Christmas pajamas adds up quickly. Luckily, your family can match on a budget. The Children’s Place has some of the best family Christmas pajamas with prices starting at under $25. And their low prices don’t mean low quality.
I’ve purchased countless sets of pajamas from The Children’s Place over the years, and I’m always impressed by how well they hold up. Last year, I bought my children matching pajamas from a big box retailer. I had to return every single pair after discovering holes along the seams and pockets after just one wash. Meanwhile, our Children’s Place pajamas are still going strong after being passed down between two or three kids.
The only thing to consider is that while they offer a ton of styles, not all of their pajamas are 100% cotton. If the material type is important to you, you’ll need to look closely at the product description for each set. That said, the Children’s Place website has a filter that lets you narrow your search to products with OEKO-TEX Standard 100 Certification.
Just keep in mind that while many styles are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 Certified, they’re not necessarily made of natural materials. You’ll still have to pay attention to the product descriptions. However, you will find a nice, affordable selection of 100% cotton pajamas for the whole family.
Our top pick: Muppets Christmas Carol
Run to Old Navy and scoop up affordable Christmas pajamas for the whole family. You can mix and match shirts, pants and shorts, which means everyone is happy, comfy and coordinated. They have an extensive selection of prints and inclusive sizing up to 4X. They even have matching accessories for your pets so the whole fam gets in on the fun.
Bandurski ordered her family Christmas pajamas from Old Navy this year and couldn’t be more excited about them. “I could not resist the Muppets Christmas Carol pattern,” she says. If you’re also smitten with this nostalgic print, choose from flannel pants and an oversized T-shirt or a matching set, all of which are made of 100% cotton. Just note that these pajamas, along with other Disney prints, are not typically included in storewide sales.
Our top pick: Knit 2-Piece Pajama Set in Winter Puffins
If you prefer a more sophisticated look, Lands’ End offers a selection of traditional plaids and prints. There are plenty of styles to choose from, including cozy flannel nightgowns and matching sets, as well as cotton nightshirts and knit pajama sets. They even carry matching robes. Lands’ End pajamas are available in a wide range of sizes for kids and adults, including regular, petite, tall and plus size. Make these Christmas pajamas extra special by personalizing each family member’s set. Add their initials, name or a logo for $10.95 per item.
Just be sure to check the brand’s sizing guide, as some reviewers note that the pajamas run large. According to Bandurski, a longtime Lands’ End fan, they do, in fact, run a bit big. “Lands’ End has been my go-to in recent history,” she says. “Their sizing is very generous, so they also fit the bill for being perfectly comfortable if not a tad too big.”
I agree with Katie. I recently ordered the Women’s Knit 2-Piece Pajama Set in the Winter Puffins pattern. I ordered my usual size, and they do indeed run big. In fact, they’re too big for my tastes, so I’ll be exchanging them for a smaller size. Otherwise, the flannel is soft, and the pattern is adorable. Perfect for the winter months!
Our top pick: Holiday Hens
Printfresh makes some of the best pajamas for women, so it’s no surprise their family pajama game is strong. We especially love the Holiday Hens pattern, which features hand-illustrated hens sporting festive scarves, earmuffs and Christmas wreaths. There are multiple silhouettes to choose from, and they’re available in sizes XXS to 6X in standard, petite and tall lengths.
Bandurski is a longtime fan of Printfresh pajamas and owns a handful of cotton and flannel sets. She notes that they run true to size, with both the top and bottom pieces offering a relaxed fit. And while they’re on the pricier side, Katie thinks they’re a worthy investment. “They wash up really nicely. I don’t typically wash them separately or with any kind of special treatment, and they still look colorful and vibrant,” she raves. “The cotton poplin sets do tend to wrinkle, though. So make sure you promptly remove them from the dryer. The flannel sets also wear nicely and get softer with every wash.”
Our top pick: Organic Cotton Fair Isle Pajamas
Have a new addition this holiday season? Carter’s Christmas jammies come in infant sizes ranging from preemie to nine months. You’ll also find plenty of styles for toddlers, kids and adults, including organic cotton and 100% cotton options. Better still, they have adorable accessories like these gingerbread man slippers to complete your look.
Over the years, I’ve purchased dozens of matching Carter’s Christmas pajamas for my children. I’ve found that they hold up well, and thanks to Carter’s frequent sales, I’m often able to get them for less than $20 per set. That said, I have found that the brand has changed quite a bit in recent years. Most notably, the toddler and big kid sizes tend to run a bit small compared to years past, so I tend to order a size up. That said, I haven’t experienced any shrinking after putting them through the washer and dryer.
Our top pick: Long-Sleeved Pajama Set in Holiday Plaid
If you prefer a coordinated look over matching styles, Kyte Baby has a lovely assortment of Christmas prints and solids to choose from. All of their pajamas are made from ultra-soft rayon from bamboo and OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified. They carry infant, children and adult sizes ranging from preemie through 3XL.
Though I haven’t ordered Kyte’s holiday pajamas, I did purchase several items for myself and my last baby almost four years ago. I still wear my now discontinued cardigan on a regular basis, and it’s held up beautifully. The baby items I had purchased went into my bin of favorite baby clothes to save for, well, forever. And I’m not the only one who loves Kyte. Mary Henn is also a fan.
“Kyte pajamas are on the pricier side, but they offer a wide range of products and prints. Kyte is known for making some of my all-time favorite clothing and pajamas for infants and toddlers. Their bamboo fabric is so, so soft, breathable and comfortable,” raves Mary. “If you’re a fan of bamboo clothing, you’ll absolutely love Kyte. The prints are also incredibly unique and artistic.”
Our top pick: Gingerbread Flurry Two-Piece Pajama Set
There’s lots to love about bamboo pajamas. They’re buttery soft, hypoallergenic, breathable and gentle on sensitive skin. Little Sleepies Christmas pajamas are made with 95% viscose from bamboo and 5% spandex. There are over a dozen patterns to choose from, and sizes range from preemie through 3XL.
What we really love about Little Sleepies is the website’s Holiday Family Matching Bundler. This feature allows you to select pajamas for one family member at a time and shows all of the available styles and sizes in one convenient place. No more toggling back and forth between pages and your cart. Talk about a pleasant shopping experience!

articles.title: Did Your Ancestors Arrive on the Mayflower? Here’s How to Find Out
articles.content:
Being related to someone who came over on the Mayflower seems like one of those things that’s easy to claim but hard to back up. Or is it?
When I got this assignment, I immediately picked up my phone and called my aunt, our family’s resident genealogist, who not only confirmed that we are indeed descended from people on the Mayflower but also rattled off the exact two passengers and their entire long line of rather prodigious offspring—right down to my dad and her.
And we are not alone by any stretch of the imagination. The same two people who spawned my family also have their DNA tentacles in millions of Americans to this very day, from former U.S. presidents to famous actors and artists to little old nobodies like me … and maybe you.
Ahead, Neil Fraser, a partner at London’s Fraser and Fraser, one of the world’s top genealogy firms, and Eva Holmes, the director of the Silver Books Project at the General Society of Mayflower Descendants, give us the history of the Mayflower descendants and explain how to find out if you have any connection to this storied boat.
Read on to learn more about this little slice of uniquely American history.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more genealogy, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
“The Mayflower carried 102 passengers, including religious Separatists who had previously left England for the Netherlands before being unsettled and planning transport to America via England,” Fraser says. “The Separatists were unhappy with the direction of the Church of England and wanted the freedom to practice their religious beliefs.”
Not everyone was so ideologically bent, though. Fraser says in addition to the Separatists, the Mayflower carried more than 20 crew members and several tradespeople and servants who were hoping for a better life.
“The overcrowded Mayflower set off alone from Plymouth [in England] in 1620 and landed in Cape Cod 66 days later,” Fraser says. “They arrived in modern-day Massachusetts in the midst of winter without shelter or supplies, and around half died during the first winter alone.”
“The Mayflower Society reckons that around 10 million Americans and 35 million people worldwide are descended from passengers on the ship,” Fraser says. You may have heard that 10% of the American population has Mayflower ties, but that’s a misconception. The current population of the U.S. is just under 350 million people, so 10 million descendants would be less than 3%.
“Even more remarkably, it is thought that only 26 men who arrived on the Mayflower have descendants,” Fraser says. “In the 406 years since the ship arrived in America, there would be between 13 and 16 generations of descendants” from the original passengers to someone who is alive today. “So the 10 million number is very achievable,” he says.
But it’s important to remember that in 400 years, there would be an “enormous number of branches on a family tree, and not all of them will have been researched or properly documented,” Fraser says. Over that many generations, records are bound to get lost, and many people just have no idea they’re related to Mayflower passengers, “so I don’t think anyone could give you an exact number.”
“This is the interesting bit,” Fraser says. “Imagine a single Mayflower couple had three children who survived and went on to have families, and each subsequent generation averaged three children who reproduced.” Through 13 generations, they’d have about 2.4 million descendants, and by generation No. 16, we’d be looking at a total of more than 64 million descendants from that single couple!
Of course, not many families reproduce quite so exponentially, but it gives you a good idea of how fast the numbers can grow. You also have to take into account the fact that family trees rarely stay isolated. “Over 400 years, cousins married cousins, sometimes without knowing they were related,” Fraser says. “The same ancestor can therefore appear in multiple branches of a family tree.”
“The remarkable feature of genealogy is that descendants multiply across generations, but family trees overlap,” Fraser adds. “Someone alive today might descend from [Mayflower passenger] John Alden through five or six different lines and from several other Mayflower passengers as well.” This overlapping is called pedigree collapse, “and it is especially relevant to early colonial New England, where relatively small communities intermarried over generations.”
Of the Mayflower families known to have had children, some were more prolific than others. Here are the ones that most likely have room for you in their crowded genealogical history.
Let’s start with the parents of my family tree: Elizabeth Tilley and John Howland. This line of Mayflower descendants reportedly has around 2 million living members, though again, the numbers are hard to quantify.
These two lovebirds did not start off married when they left England. John Howland was a servant who was nearly killed on the voyage, and Elizabeth Tilley was a teenager whose parents both died during the first winter at Plymouth, leaving her an orphan. They eventually married and had 10 children and 88 grandchildren, Fraser says.
“John Howland’s story is quite remarkable because he was actually swept overboard during the voyage and survived by grabbing hold of a rope,” Fraser says. “Had he not survived, generations of American descendants who came after him would never have existed.” (Thanks for having a good grip, John!)
Here’s another family tree that likely holds millions of members. “John Alden and Priscilla Mullins are among the Mayflower passengers believed to have some of the best documented descendant populations,” Fraser says. “It is thought that after arriving in America, they had 10 recorded children, and seven of them went on to have surviving descendants.”
Alden was a crew member on the Mayflower, signing up to be the ship’s cooper (aka barrel maker). articles.title: Here’s the Real Reason Frankenstein’s Creature Is Green—And a Monster of Few Words
articles.content:
Think you know everything about Frankenstein’s creation? Think again. Sure, you know the guy: green skin, bolts in his neck and a face that could scare the life out of you. Oh, and a vocabulary that doesn’t go much beyond a few grunts. But here’s a Halloween trick for you: Just about everything you picture when you think of Frankenstein’s creature is different from what Mary Shelley originally dreamed up. So how did we get from her famous novel to the monster we know today? Turns out, Hollywood gave the big guy a little makeover.
To help us separate Hollywood’s scary version of Frankenstein’s monster from Shelley’s original creation, we spoke with Andrew Scahill, PhD, an assistant film professor at the University of Colorado Denver. As it turns out, the creature has quite the backstory. In fact, according to Scahill, “Shelley’s creature could probably hold his own in your book club.” Who would have thought?
Read on to find out how the creature we know today came to be, and why there’s more to him than meets the eye.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more history, holidays, fun facts, entertainment, humor, travel and tech all week long.
“It started with some very literary people trying to entertain themselves during terrible weather,” says Scahill. The year was 1816, and 18-year-old Mary Godwin (soon to be Mary Shelley) was spending the summer near Lake Geneva with a group that included her future husband, Percy Shelley, and the poet Lord Byron. When Byron challenged everyone to come up with a ghost story, she initially drew a blank. Then came a waking vision of a student watching a body he’d pieced together come to life. That was the spark for Frankenstein, which was published anonymously on Jan. 1, 1818, when Shelley was just 20.
If it’s been a while since you’ve read the book, here’s a refresher: Victor Frankenstein is a scientist who figures out how to bring a creature (made of body parts from corpses) to life, only to recoil in horror at what he’s created. But there’s a twist. “Victor has already told us what to think of him, and then this supposedly loathsome being begins describing his first experiences of the world,” Scahill says. “Cold. Hunger. The pleasure of birdsong. We have to spend time with him.” Suddenly, it’s not so easy to decide who’s the real monster here. After all, as Scahill puts it, Victor “has brought someone into the world and immediately made his own disappointment that person’s problem.” Talk about a rough start to life.
Shelley’s original creature looked nothing like the monster you see on Halloween decorations. “Very little of that familiar image survives a reading of the novel,” says Scahill. “He is yellow-skinned, fast and extraordinarily strong.” He is also roughly 8 feet tall, and “his skin barely covers the muscles and arteries underneath.” But Victor had actually tried to make his creation attractive. “The hair and teeth are lovely,” Scahill explains. “Everything together is unbearable to him.”
And there’s another wrinkle to this description. We’re seeing the creature through the eyes of the very man who brought him to life and immediately regretted it. “We tend to receive it as an objective inventory of what’s wrong with the creature,” Scahill says. “But we are also hearing a parent describe a child he wishes he hadn’t made.” It makes you wonder whether the creature was really quite as horrifying as Victor made him out to be.
You can thank Hollywood for that one. Well, mostly. The green-faced monster we know today owes much of his look to Universal’s 1931 film Frankenstein, starring Boris Karloff as the creature. But the unusual skin color really goes back further than that—and has its roots in the theater. “An unnatural complexion predates Karloff by more than a century,” says Scahill. In fact, an 1823 stage adaptation called Presumption described the creature’s skin as “light blue or French gray.” Meanwhile, the National Library of Medicine has described actor T.P. Cooke’s stage portrayal as having a green face and blue body paint. “Those accounts don’t quite agree, so I wouldn’t turn them into a neat origin story,” Scahill notes.
Fast-forward to 1931, when makeup artist Jack Pierce was tasked with bringing Karloff’s monster to life. He used greenish, or gray-green, makeup, even though the movie was filmed in black and white. Why bother with color? It all came down to how makeup appeared on camera. “Black-and-white film doesn’t respond to every color in the same way,” Scahill explains. Different shades could appear lighter or darker depending on the film stock and lighting. “Something quite odd in the dressing-room mirror could look convincing on screen.” In this case, Pierce wanted Karloff to look as though the life had been drained right out of him. “The audience needed to feel that something was wrong with this skin, even though they couldn’t see the color he was actually wearing.”
And Pierce didn’t stop at the skin. He also gave the creature that unmistakable flat head. “Pierce worked backward from the imaginary operation,” Scahill says. “How would this man have got a brain into that head?” The makeup artist imagined Frankenstein cutting open the skull, inserting a brain and fastening everything back together. That explains the scar across the forehead and the metal clamps. As for those famous neck bolts? They’re generally understood to be electrodes.
To pull off the look, Pierce built up Karloff’s head using cotton and collodion, a liquid that hardens as it dries. He added heavy eyelids, while the costume’s shortened sleeves made Karloff’s arms appear unusually long. The result was a far cry from Shelley’s original description. And yet, as Scahill points out, “the face looks handled, altered, damaged. It also looks hurt.” Not bad for a few hours in the makeup chair.
“The film was black and white. The things you could buy weren’t,” Scahill says. “Magazine covers, model kits, Halloween masks—all those versions of the creature needed a complexion, and green became the familiar choice.” Before long, that green face was everywhere.
And television helped keep it that way. In 1957, Screen Gems began distributing Universal’s classic monster movies to TV stations, introducing the creature to a whole new audience. Then came Aurora’s Frankenstein model kit in 1961, followed by The Munsters, which turned a Frankenstein-inspired monster into a sitcom dad. Even though the show aired in black and white, the 1966 movie Munster, Go Home! let audiences see Herman Munster in full color.
All that exposure helped cement the look, especially for kids who grew up seeing the monster on everything from toys to Halloween costumes. “I think we underestimate how often we encounter these characters through their souvenirs,” Scahill says. “A child can know exactly what Frankenstein looks like years before finding out what happened to him.” By then, imagining him as any other color was pretty much out of the question.
Here’s another shocker: Shelley’s creature isn’t some lumbering brute who can barely string two words together. He’s actually intelligent, well-read and quite the talker. So how did he go from delivering thoughtful speeches to mostly grunting his way through Hollywood? According to Scahill, “that happened on stage first. Peake’s 1823 creature was speechless, so Hollywood inherited a performance tradition built around gesture and movement.” And while Karloff’s monster did pick up a few words in 1935’s Bride of Frankenstein, his silence became one of his defining traits.
But that’s hardly the only liberty Hollywood took with Shelley’s story. Here’s what else might surprise you:
And here’s where things come full circle. Guillermo del Toro’s 2025 Frankenstein, starring Jacob Elordi as the creature, gives him back something many movie versions have denied him: his voice. “Elordi’s creature gets to develop, to learn and to describe what has happened to him,” Scahill says. But don’t mistake it for a completely faithful retelling. Del Toro gives Victor and his creation a chance at forgiveness, while Shelley’s novel ends with the creature speaking over his creator’s dead body. As Scahill puts it: “All that eloquence, and the person who most needed to hear it is gone.”
Oh, and one last thing about so many people calling the monster Frankenstein. Scahill isn’t bothered by it. “If we read the creature as Victor’s abandoned son, why shouldn’t he have his father’s name?” he says. “I like the idea that the culture has given him something Victor refused to offer. Calling him Frankenstein is a mistake that tells the truth.”

Why bother with color? It all came down to how makeup appeared on camera. “Black-and-white film doesn’t respond to every color in the same way,” Scahill explains. Different shades could appear lighter or darker depending on the film stock and lighting. “Something quite odd in the dressing-room mirror could look convincing on screen.” In this case, Pierce wanted Karloff to look as though the life had been drained right out of him. “The audience needed to feel that something was wrong with this skin, even though they couldn’t see the color he was actually wearing.”

And Pierce didn’t stop at the skin. He also gave the creature that unmistakable flat head. “Pierce worked backward from the imaginary operation,” Scahill says. “How would this man have got a brain into that head?” The makeup artist imagined Frankenstein cutting open the skull, inserting a brain and fastening everything back together. That explains the scar across the forehead and the metal clamps. As for those famous neck bolts? They’re generally understood to be electrodes.

To pull off the look, Pierce built up Karloff’s head using cotton and collodion, a liquid that hardens as it dries. He added heavy eyelids, while the costume’s shortened sleeves made Karloff’s arms appear unusually long. The result was a far cry from Shelley’s original description. And yet, as Scahill points out, “the face looks handled, altered, damaged. It also looks hurt.” Not bad for a few hours in the makeup chair.

Why did this green hue become a Frankenstein staple after this?

“The film was black and white. The things you could buy weren’t,” Scahill says. “Magazine covers, model kits, Halloween masks—all those versions of the creature needed a complexion, and green became the familiar choice.” Before long, that green face was everywhere.

And television helped keep it that way. In 1957, Screen Gems began distributing Universal’s classic monster movies to TV stations, introducing the creature to a whole new audience. Then came Aurora’s Frankenstein model kit in 1961, followed by The Munsters, which turned a Frankenstein-inspired monster into a sitcom dad. Even though the show aired in black and white, the 1966 movie Munster, Go Home! let audiences see Herman Munster in full color.

All that exposure helped cement the look, especially for kids who grew up seeing the monster on everything from toys to Halloween costumes. “I think we underestimate how often we encounter these characters through their souvenirs,” Scahill says. “A child can know exactly what Frankenstein looks like years before finding out what happened to him.” By then, imagining him as any other color was pretty much out of the question.

What else about the creature is vastly different in the book vs. the majority of pop-culture representations?

Here’s another shocker: Shelley’s creature isn’t some lumbering brute who can barely string two words together. He’s actually intelligent, well-read and quite the talker. So how did he go from delivering thoughtful speeches to mostly grunting his way through Hollywood? According to Scahill, “that happened on stage first. Peake’s 1823 creature was speechless, so Hollywood inherited a performance tradition built around gesture and movement.” And while Karloff’s monster did pick up a few words in 1935’s Bride of Frankenstein, his silence became one of his defining traits.

But that’s hardly the only liberty Hollywood took with Shelley’s story. Here’s what else might surprise you:

  • He’s not just a mindless killer. In the 1931 film, Karloff’s creature accidentally drowns a little girl after tossing her into a lake, believing she’ll float like the flowers they’ve been playing with. Shelley’s version is far more deliberate. “Shelley’s creature deliberately strangles William, knowing he belongs to the Frankenstein family,” Scahill says. “Those are very different things to ask an audience to reckon with.”
  • He doesn’t have a criminal’s brain. Remember the whole mix-up involving the origin of his brain? That’s a Hollywood invention. “The 1931 film gives the creature an abnormal brain taken from a criminal, so there’s a ready explanation for his violence inside his skull,” Scahill explains. “In the novel, we have to work through his experiences and his choices.”
  • There’s no Igor. Sorry, Igor fans. “Victor works alone,” Scahill says. The assistant Fritz appeared in the stage tradition and the 1931 film, while Bela Lugosi’s memorable character didn’t arrive until 1939’s Son of Frankenstein.
  • The famous electrical laboratory isn’t in the book. All those crackling machines and dramatic switches? More movie magic. “Shelley also withholds the precise method of animation,” Scahill says. “The elaborate electrical laboratory supplies a spectacle where the book leaves a gap.”
  • The creature never gets his bride. While Hollywood gave us Bride of Frankenstein, things play out differently in the book. Victor begins making a female companion but destroys her before bringing her to life.

And here’s where things come full circle. Guillermo del Toro’s 2025 Frankenstein, starring Jacob Elordi as the creature, gives him back something many movie versions have denied him: his voice. “Elordi’s creature gets to develop, to learn and to describe what has happened to him,” Scahill says. But don’t mistake it for a completely faithful retelling. Del Toro gives Victor and his creation a chance at forgiveness, while Shelley’s novel ends with the creature speaking over his creator’s dead body. As Scahill puts it: “All that eloquence, and the person who most needed to hear it is gone.”

Oh, and one last thing about so many people calling the monster Frankenstein. Scahill isn’t bothered by it. “If we read the creature as Victor’s abandoned son, why shouldn’t he have his father’s name?” he says. “I like the idea that the culture has given him something Victor refused to offer. Calling him Frankenstein is a mistake that tells the truth.”

If you’ve spent any time on social media, you’ve likely heard about “cortisol face,” “Ozempic face” and even “runner’s face.” If you’re not familiar, here’s a little spoiler: These are not flattering terms. Newer to the bunch is “ferritin face,” which has loads of TikTok videos devoted to it that date back to at least 2024. But the term really took off last summer.
Ferritin face is characterized by a few distinct signs that make you look bone-tired. As a working single mom of two, there are many mornings when I can relate to this look, unfortunately. Chances are, you might too … but is the reason for your less-than-sunny appearance because of this supposed condition, which has its root in an actual medical condition? Or is the internet getting ahead of itself again?
We decided to do a little research of our own to find out if this TikTok diagnosis is the real deal. Read on to learn how to identify so-called ferritin face and and what to do if it uncovers a larger health problem for you.

Ferritin face is the TikTok name for a generally tired appearance featuring dark under-eye circles and pale or sallow skin, resulting from low iron levels. In other words, if you’re exhibiting these signs, you might not be the regular kind of tired; you may have an iron deficiency. At least according to the many (many) videos currently going around TikTok, like this one with more than 100,000 views, in which the creator notes that her pale lips indicated more than she initially realized.
This social media term takes its inspiration from a protein named—you guessed it—ferritin, which binds to iron and stores it so the body can make red blood cells. Since the human body doesn’t make its own iron, we have to consume it. When iron levels are low, it can be because we’re not getting it in our diet or because our body isn’t absorbing it properly.
“People say you are what you eat, but you’re actually what you absorb,” says Caitlin Hosmer, a licensed dietitian nutritionist, a clinician at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and the co-founder of Meno Pantry. “You can put things into your mouth, but if they don’t get out of your digestive system and into your body, you’re not absorbing them. Absorption issues can be a cause of low iron and can lead to deficiency over time.”
“Like a lot of things on social media, there’s a little kernel of truth,” Hosmer says. “The troubling piece is the way information gets spread.”
Scott Nass, MD, a family medicine physician at SwiftCareMD, agrees. “Low iron may make a person appear pale in certain areas of the body, such as the mouth area or inner portion of the lower eyelid. However, health-care professionals cannot determine a patient’s ferritin levels by observing facial appearance.” Plus, that pale skin is just one symptom of low iron levels—and not even the most telltale sign. “Fatigue is usually the most noticeable symptom,” Dr. Nass explains. “Many other symptoms can also be present.”
Those other symptoms include:
The bottom line: Just because your skin is washed out and looks like you need a vacation ASAP, it doesn’t mean you’re iron deficient. “In addition to anemia, other factors such as poor sleep patterns, dehydration, light exposure and a person’s normal skin tone may create facial appearances similar to what a physician might see with low ferritin,” Dr. Nass says.
When your body doesn’t have enough iron, it causes iron-deficiency anemia. Besides the symptoms of low iron noted above, this could also lead to problems with your cardiovascular and immune systems—from heart palpitations and shortness of breath to an impaired ability to fight infection. If your iron levels are too low, your physician might prescribe an iron supplement.
But before you run to the drugstore to get your own iron supplement, well, don’t. Dr. Nass and Hosmer say it’s essential not to start taking iron on your own without guidance. Too much iron isn’t a good thing either. The body stores excess iron, rather than getting rid of it, and those makeshift storage spots include various organs that iron can damage or even cause to fail over time.
A mirror won’t tell you that your iron levels are low—only a blood test can do that.
If you suspect you have low iron, talk to your doctor and ask for a blood test to check your levels. While hemoglobin and hematocrit in red blood cells are measured in a standard complete blood count (CBC), you might need to request for your ferritin to be tested as well.
For starters, know your risks. Vegans and vegetarians are more susceptible to iron deficiencies because they don’t consume the main sources of heme iron: seafood and meat. Women are also at a higher risk of an iron deficiency until their menstrual cycles stop at menopause. Their recommended daily allowance (RDA) for iron is much higher than men’s until that point: It’s 18 milligrams per day for women ages 19 to 50, and 8 milligrams for adult men and women 51 and older.
If you want to boost your iron levels, Hosmer recommends doing so with food first. The top sources of iron are (surprisingly) 100% iron-fortified breakfast cereals, oysters, beef and chicken. Iron is in plant sources, like legumes, tofu and vegetables, but it’s non-heme, meaning not as much of it gets absorbed as heme iron.
Whatever you do, don’t self-diagnose from TikTok videos. “It is dangerous to immediately take iron just because some video seems to relate to your current state,” Dr. Nass says. But if your energy levels have been consistently low and you’ve also been sporting sallow skin and under-eye circles that just won’t go away, don’t ignore it. This knowledge could be the nudge you need to make that long-overdue doctor’s appointment.

articles.title: Those SMS Codes You Use to Log In to Your Accounts Are on Their Way Out—Here’s What You’ll Need to Do Instead
articles.content:
We all know the drill. You go to log into your bank, work email or favorite news website only to be met with a little pop-up blocking your access until you input an SMS code, a form of two-factor authentication. Would you like that code sent to your phone via text or email? Is your phone even near you, or charged? Well, you’d better hurry! It expires in 10 minutes.
Now, just when we finally got used to logging in this way, big changes are coming. (Sigh.) In fact, they’re here already for one major company, at least for many of its products and sites. And you know how it goes in the tech world: Once one company does something, it’s only a matter of time before they all jump on the train.
Ahead, I’ll walk you through the latest change to online security measures, tell you what’s replacing SMS verifications and explain how the new paradigm will affect you going forward. Keep reading to learn more and get ahead of the changing tech landscape.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, entertainment, humor and fun facts all week long.
Not yet. Microsoft is leading the charge here. The company recently announced that the familiar text codes will be phased out for personal Microsoft accounts, including Outlook, MSN and Hotmail, as well as other Windows applications and products like XBox, Windows PCs and Skype.
In addition to personal accounts, Microsoft announced the impending retirement of SMS codes for organizations that use Microsoft products. If you use Outlook or another MS product at work or school, you may have already begun seeing this change.
Other companies that are encouraging users to move away from SMS authentication include OpenAI, which announced earlier this year that users will be given the option to switch to another form of verification, and Google, which still supports SMS codes but is also pushing users to use other options.
It’s all about security. According to Microsoft, SMS verification is a huge source of fraud. The thing is, text messages are not that secure—telephone and cellular networks were just not designed to keep information sent in plain-text messages out of prying eyes.
And scammers have several ways to trick you into giving up your code. The biggest one is called SIM-card swapping. This is when fraudsters convince a mobile carrier to transfer your SIM card to them, log in to your accounts and intercept the SMS code that is sent for authentication. A Texas man was just convicted of this kind of fraud, sentenced to 70 months in prison and ordered to pay $1.7 million in restitution to victims. Last year, a Florida man was sentenced to 10 years in prison for similar crimes involving 59 separate victims. According to the FBI, this kind of SMS fraud cost consumers $26 million in 2024.
Aside from SIM-card swapping, relying on text messages to verify your account credentials sets you up for phishing attacks. Scammers set up a fake page that looks like your bank, email or other account, then send you a text message to entice you to log in to the fake page. They capture your info, log in themselves and have you enter the SMS code that is sent to you. Text-message fraud cost consumers $470 million in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).
Microsoft is starting to use passkeys instead of SMS codes. Passkeys are forms of multi-factor authentication that include Face ID, fingerprints or a special digital key that uses your device to prove it’s really you. They work through something called “public-key cryptography,” a private key that’s stored on your device (like your fingerprint or Face ID), and a public key that comes from the website you’re trying to log in to.
When you log in to your accounts, the private key and the public key challenge each other to verify that you are authorized to log in. So instead of using a password or code that goes out over an insecure text, your device itself stores the info and proves that the public key and private key match. Passkeys are resistant to fraud because they cannot be faked by external actors.
It’s easy. When you log in to your Microsoft account, you will be prompted to create a passkey. (It’s currently optional on personal accounts, so you can also choose to skip the new process for now.)
Here’s what to do:
Now what? The next time you attempt to sign in to your Microsoft account, you will not receive that SMS-code prompt or that 10-minute countdown. Instead, you’ll be asked to provide the passkey you created directly on your phone or device, whether that’s your Face ID, fingerprint, PIN or security key.
Microsoft is already phasing out the old SMS codes, so you’ve likely seen the prompt window when you log in. For workplaces and other organizations, Microsoft plans to have everyone moved over to passkeys by July 2027. But the company has not made a public announcement about when the old codes will be 100% obsolete for personal accounts.
So for now, you can continue to ignore the prompt to create a passkey. But after learning how easy it is for scammers to infiltrate your accounts using SMS codes, you might want to create one sooner rather than later.
